description:
We are students who treat a hackathon like real engineering: one finished scenario, honest numbers, no overpromising. In two days the three of us built LUCY: from choosing NASA data (LOLA terrain, JPL DE440) to a deterministic calculation core, a map, calendar, site comparison, 3D view and demo video. Every number comes from a real source.

Our motto: "Larp everything you can."
summary:
LUCY (Lunar Uptime & Communication Yardstick) is a scientific web application designed to evaluate operational conditions for potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. Using NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) terrain data and JPL DE440 ephemerides, LUCY calculates when the Sun and Earth are visible from a selected location, accounting for the surrounding lunar terrain and the Moon’s curvature.

Users can analyze specific locations and dates, evaluate mission requirements, compare multiple sites, and search for locations and time windows that meet defined constraints. The application provides practical metrics, including longest periods of darkness, sunlight availability, and communication gaps caused by loss of direct Earth visibility. It also features interactive terrain maps and 3D site visualization.

All visibility and mission assessments are performed using deterministic mathematical calculations, without SI-generated results or external API dependencies. LUCY helps explore the relationship between lunar terrain, solar power availability, and direct-to-Earth communication when evaluating potential lunar mission sites.

LUCY shows acceptable landing windows based on illumination and direct Earth visibility; it does not guarantee mission success.
details:
What it does. Near the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and terrain casts long shadows, so a landing site needs both sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication. LUCY answers one question: could a lander operate here, on this date? The user picks a point near the pole, a start date and a mission profile (window length, longest acceptable night, longest acceptable communication gap, minimum Sun share, instrument height). LUCY returns a clear verdict, plain metrics (longest night, Sun share, longest and total time without Earth) and a one-sentence explanation of the result.

Features. (1) Site analysis with daily Sun and Earth charts and a minute-by-minute visibility timeline. (2) The nearest acceptable window for a site within five years. (3) Reverse search: where and when a landing is possible for the chosen mission conditions, over a 5 km grid covering a 154 km zone around the pole. (4) Side-by-side comparison of up to three sites. (5) A 3D view of the terrain around the site, seen from outside or from the lander. (6) Four example scenarios that show every kind of outcome. Any date from 2000 to 2050 can be calculated live.

How it works. The calculation is deterministic and reproducible. It contains no SI and no estimates by eye. For each site, a horizon profile (720 azimuth sectors, 150 km radius) is computed from the NASA LOLA 80 m south pole elevation model, with the Moon’s curvature included in the 3D geometry. Skyfield and the JPL DE440 ephemeris give the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth, rotated into the lunar body-fixed frame that matches the LOLA terrain. A body counts as visible when its altitude is above the terrain horizon in its azimuth. Visibility is evaluated on a continuous 1-minute grid, because an hourly grid misses events shorter than an hour. Mission logic then checks each window against the thresholds.

Verification. Sun and Earth directions were checked against the independent JPL Horizons service (54 directions at three sites). The largest difference is 0.000022 degrees. The reference values are stored in the repository, and the result is shown in the interface.

Benefits and impact. Mission planners, students and researchers can see the trade-off between power and communication directly, without reading raw data. The metrics are the thresholds themselves, with no arbitrary combined score. The explanation for every result is a single sentence.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio and Skyfield on the backend. The frontend is vanilla JavaScript with hand-drawn SVG maps and charts, plus Three.js for the 3D view. There are no build tools or frameworks. The demo runs on our own server (Caddy, systemd). Terrain and ephemeris files are stored on its disk, and all positions are computed locally, so the working path makes no external API calls.

What is creative. The reverse search and the multi-site comparison turn a one-site calculator into a site-selection tool. The nearest-window finder and the example scenarios make results quick to understand.

Factors considered. Accuracy first: real NASA data, a verified ephemeris and 1-minute resolution. Honesty second: the tool shows allowed landing windows, not a guarantee of mission success. Limitations are stated in the project. The Sun and Earth are treated as points at the body centre, eclipses are not modelled, and communication means direct line of sight with no relay satellites. The example scenarios are not recommendations of landing sites. The project is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

Use of SI. The code, tests and documentation of this project were written with the help of Super Intelligence (SI) tools, under our direction: the goals, the rules and every decision were set by the team, and we reviewed the results. The calculation of Sun and Earth visibility, night length, communication gaps and landing windows contains no SI. It is plain, deterministic mathematics on real data (LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides), and the same inputs always give the same result.

Open source. Code and documentation are in the public repository under the MIT license. Source: https://github.com/globalsurveygpt-beep/ultraLarpProject
